teaser: A dress, a shampoo bottle, an album cover: they all borrowed from this small square.

lesson.text: In 1965 the Paris designer Yves Saint Laurent sent six shift dresses down the runway. White wool, black bands, a block of red, a block of blue, a block of yellow. Fashion magazines called them the Mondrian dresses, and soon the same pattern was on bags, kitchen tiles and hair-product bottles.

The painter never saw any of it. Piet Mondrian had died in New York in 1944. What the world copied was a kind of picture he made over and over in his Paris studio around 1930, and this canvas, only about 46 centimeters (18 inches) square, is one of the purest versions.

Saint Laurent's dresses were not printed. Each colored block was a separate piece of wool jersey, sewn to its neighbors with the seams hidden inside the black bands, so the dress hung as flat as a painting.

Why did this particular arrangement stick in everyone's memory? Part of the answer is how little there is. Three colors, each used once. Five black lines. The rest is white. With so few pieces, the placement of each one has to be exactly right.
Three drawn lines show how the surface is organized.

lines.label: The long vertical
lines.text: It runs the full height and sits far to the left, about a quarter of the way in. Nothing here is centered.

lines.label: The long horizontal
lines.text: It crosses low, about three quarters of the way down. Together the two lines cut one huge field in the upper right and leave three narrow zones around it.

lines.label: Three colors, three corners
lines.text: Join the red, the blue and the yellow and you get a lopsided triangle. The two small colors sit low and far apart, like two feet holding up the red.

lesson.text: The red fills roughly half the canvas. It also touches the top and right edges with no black line to close it in, so it seems to keep going past the frame. The blue and the yellow, by contrast, are boxed into the bottom corners. Big and open against small and enclosed.

Mondrian painted all of this by hand, slowly, in many layers. He would shift a line by a few millimeters, step back, and shift it again. Friends described weeks spent on a single canvas that seems, to a hurried eye, as if it took an afternoon.

He loved dancing. In 1920s Paris, the stern-looking Dutchman in the tidy suit went out to jazz clubs to dance the foxtrot and the Charleston, and he compared the rhythm of jazz to the rhythm he wanted in his paintings.
The hand shows if you get near enough. The black lines are not all the same width, and the white is not one white. The camera will take you to four places where the “machine-made” look falls apart.

lesson.title: Made by hand
lesson.text: From a distance this seems printed. Up close it is clearly a painting.

spots.title: A thick bar
spots.text: This horizontal band on the left is about twice as wide as the long line under the red. Mondrian tuned each width separately, the way you adjust the volume of each instrument.

spots.title: The stub
spots.text: A short, heavy black block sits on top of the yellow like a lid. It makes the tiny yellow corner feel dense enough to answer the huge red.

spots.title: Cracked white
spots.text: Fine cracks run through the white paint. He built his whites up in thick layers, and after nearly a century they have aged like the glaze on old porcelain.

spots.title: PM 30
spots.text: His initials and the year, brushed in dark paint straight onto the blue. Even the signature is placed so it disturbs the balance as little as possible.

lesson.text: One more thing is visible at the outer border: a pale strip around the canvas. Mondrian disliked heavy gilded frames that turn a picture into a window. He mounted his canvases so they stand slightly forward from a plain, set-back frame, entering the room like an object.

In 1930 the American sculptor Alexander Calder visited Mondrian's studio, where colored cardboard rectangles were pinned to the white walls. Calder said the sight made him want to see those rectangles move. Soon after, he began making the hanging sculptures we call mobiles.

So the echoes started early, and they never stopped. The rock duo The White Stripes named their 2000 album “De Stijl” after the Dutch group Mondrian had belonged to, and dressed its cover in red, white and black planes.
Balance without a subject can fool even experts. In 2022 a curator showed that another Mondrian, “New York City I”, had most likely been hanging upside down in museums for decades.
A design this spare is easy to copy and very hard to invent. Move the blue two fingers to the right and the picture would stop holding together.

quiz.question: Who turned Mondrian's style into a famous dress in 1965?
quiz.explanation: Saint Laurent showed six Mondrian dresses in his 1965 collection.

quiz.question: Where does the long vertical line sit?
options: About a quarter of the way in from the left
quiz.explanation: It stands far to the left; nothing in the picture is centered.

quiz.question: Why does the red seem to continue beyond the canvas?
options: It touches the top and right edges with no line closing it
It is painted on the frame
It is repeated in all four corners
quiz.explanation: No black line encloses the red at the top or on the right.

quiz.question: Which sculptor was inspired by a visit to Mondrian's studio in 1930?
quiz.explanation: Calder wanted to see the rectangles move, and went on to make mobiles.

quiz.question: What can you see in the white areas up close?
quiz.explanation: The layered white paint has developed fine cracks with age.

facts.text: All the black lines in this painting have the same width.
facts.explanation: The bar on the left is about twice as thick as the long horizontal line.

facts.text: Mondrian liked to go dancing to jazz in Paris.
facts.explanation: He danced the foxtrot and the Charleston and linked jazz rhythm to his painting.

facts.text: Mondrian personally approved the Yves Saint Laurent dresses.
facts.explanation: He died in 1944, more than twenty years before the dresses appeared.
